activity: flats disaster at Canning Town, the collapse of Ronan Point

te.text: Housing--Accidents--Flats Disaster at Canning Town, London. May 1968

IN THE tragedy of Ronan Point
yesterday, the only blessing was
that it happened too early to
become a full-scale disaster.

Too early. At 5.45 am., to be exact.
Too early for the families in the 22-
storey block of East End flats to be
up and busying themselves in their
sitting-rooms.

For, miraculously, it was 22 identical
living rooms which collapsed, in the
inevitable simile, "like a pack of cards."

In 22 identical bedrooms, families were
shocked, shattered, scared and totally be-
wildered. But, most of them, they escaped
the avalanche that thundered past their
bedroom doors.

'MATTER OF PROVIDENCE'

As Home Secretary Mr. James Callaghan
said on his tour of inspection: "It was
obviously a matter of providence that these
people were not in their living rooms."

A policeman was more blunt: "If it had
happened an hour later, the death roll
would have been very much higher," he said.

So, quite amazingly, the death roll was
infinitely less than anyone could have
hoped. And in nearby houses, and a school
where those who escaped gathered, as if still
seeking mutual protection, the survivors
wonderingly told the tales which will live
with them for the rest of their lives.

There was 56-year-old Miss Ivy Hodge, in
whose 18th floor kitchen it is believed the
collapse started. "I was putting the kettle
on," she said, "and the next moment I was
on the floor. There were flames everywhere
and I remember staggering to the door of
my flat so that someone could help me."

Somebody did. Miss Hodge was taken to
hospital and treated for burns.

There was Mr. James Chambers and his
wife Beatrice, aged 62, who were asleep in
their 7th floor flat. He said: "Suddenly our
bedroom wall fell away with a terrible rip-
ping sound. And we found ourselves staring
out over London...
